cards.explanation: The answer is his own judgment. Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus (1 Corinthians 1:1), says it plainly: “…I have no command from the Lord, but I give a judgment as one who by the Lord’s mercy is trustworthy.” He tells you right up front which kind of advice you're getting. I wish every recipe came with that kind of honesty, friends.
The answer is “Do not seek to be released.” Paul asks, “Are you committed to a wife?” and answers right away with those words. Short question, short answer, friends. He doesn't dress it up.
The answer is False. Paul asks, “Are you free of commitment?” and then says, “Do not look for a wife.” He is not sending anybody out to go look, friends. The verse says the exact opposite.
The answer is False. Paul says, “And if a virgin marries, she has not sinned.” He says the same about the man who marries. Marrying isn't the problem in this verse, friends.

The answer is troubles. Paul says, “But those who marry will face troubles in this life, and I want to spare you this.” He isn't calling marriage a sin, because he just said they haven't sinned. He's being honest that troubles come with it, and he'd like to spare them.

The answer is True. Paul says, “From now on those who have wives should live as if they had none…” It comes right after he says the time is short. It's a bold line, friends, and it's exactly what he wrote.

The answer is that this world's present form is passing away. Paul says, “For this world in its present form is passing away.” That's the reason he gives, friends, for using the things of this world as if not dependent on them.

The answer is the work of the Lord. Paul says, “The unmarried man is concerned about the work of the Lord, how he can please the Lord.” It's right there in verse 32, friends. He's putting the two kinds of men side by side.

The two answers are wife and divided. Paul says the married man is concerned about “…the affairs of this world, how he can please his wife…” and that his “…interests are divided.” Look at what sits on each side, friends. The unmarried man is concerned about “…the work of the Lord…” I think that's the split Paul is pointing at: two sets of concerns, both asking for the same man's attention.
The answer is in both body and spirit. Paul says the unmarried woman or virgin is concerned about “…how she can be holy in both body and spirit.” Both parts are in the verse, friends.

The answer is False. Paul says, “But the married woman is concerned about the affairs of this world, how she can please her husband.” The work of the Lord is what he says about the unmarried woman or virgin. He lines the two up side by side, friends.

The answer is True. Paul says, “I am saying this for your own good, not to restrict you, but in order to promote proper decorum and undivided devotion to the Lord.” That's his reason, friends, in his own words. He says it's for their good, and he says it's not meant to restrict them.
The answer is that he is not sinning. Paul says, “…let him do as he wishes; he is not sinning; they should get married.” He doesn't leave any doubt on that, friends.

The answer is True. Paul describes a man who is “…firmly established in his heart and under no constraint, with control over his will and resolve in his heart not to marry the virgin…” Of that man Paul says, “…he will do well.” That's verse 37, friends, and all those conditions come before it.
The answer is better. Paul writes, “So then, he who marries the virgin does well, but he who does not marry her does even better.” Notice, friends, that both men are doing well in his words.
The answer is True. Paul says, “But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord.” The one condition, friends, is that last part.

The answer is the Spirit of God. Paul closes with, “And I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” He says “I think” there, friends, and I bet that's him giving his judgment, like he said back in verse 25.
